yeah I'm curious how similar it actually is, I feel like it would maybe make some sense if I looked at how NFC actually works tho

From memory the process goes like this:
-Enable MCU
-Configure MCU to talk with the NFC reader
-Wait until NFC reader is ready
-Start NFC polling for data
-Check if any tag is present. Repeat until is true
-Send read request / Send write request
-Wait until request is ready and read the buffer / Write data to buffer
-Stop polling for data
subcmd 5 is actually get NFC status. It returns a bunch of data like what the nfc module is doing. Which tags are nearby and if connection is lost
You can request that at any time within the steps

NFC is read an written in memory blocks. Each block is 4  bytes. Here is an example to a read request which is subcmd 0x06
```Switch2 Protocol Data
    CommandLength: 0x13
    CommandBuffer: d007000000000000000103003b3c7778860000
    McuUnk: 0xd0
    McuUIDLength: 7
    McuUID: 00000000000000
    McuTagType: 1 (NTAG 215)
    McuBlockCount: 3
    McuReadBlock: 00-3b, 3c-77, 78-86
    Command: 0x06 (MCU read device)
    ReportType: 0x01 (MCU)
    ReportMode: 0x91 (Request)```
Which reads 3 regions 00-3b, 3c-77, 78-86. Basically the full tag. The data is sectioned in block regions because you can't fit it all in the buffer
ah that checks out then
This part is easy to match because we have a lot of know magic numbers
However subcmds like 0x03, 0x04 that have no arguments well is a bit more difficult. Since we can't test command by command with homebrew

On write is the other way around although you don't write the full tag since some parts are memory protected. So your memory regions are 05-20, 20-f0, 5c-98
```Switch2 Protocol Data
    McuBlock0Data: 6a67ab1ed93fce3b52667b3135f851bbbc38cf9c66bcac2c072b3fe3a9ac68a6
    McuBlock1Data […]: d8ef6bba6c4d8253b67f25160c97089bed301cf3276895133aca673e20668aa817258838626f4a71097a14d7478486ef5a93d4043f02dca6409cf0fc6ef24630c28d7e4c1e359c0e43214a16c779120e68d56b4bbf1d3f78de0ec9aba8f936de1c0351433ad34afedf196db0fe
    McuBlock2Data […]: bee051cba89e16954e0bddf3680541ee3ac27dcf7e257277df3e92b81d0b7f7d58278379bb76758732dc8f601f48c8ed2da76f4e1ca0cedb4e044cb3cde58dd36b2e5310ab8ffc6b57990e44695a2187664cb4ed15934e2f62c15610c067c0192b3a7f67fa182653e9ed1730a8
    McuWriteBlock: 05-20, 20-f0, 5c-98
    McuBlockCount: 3
    McuUIDLength: 7
    McuUID: 048e2f4ab75d80
    McuTagType: 1 (NTAG 215)
    Command: 0x08 (MCU write device)
    ReportType: 0x01 (MCU)
    ReportMode: 0x91 (Request)```

From what I read, I think it's a bit of a stretch to call HD Rumble ADPCM audio. Yes there are split bands and yes it works in steps, but from what I can remember there are only two perfect sinusodal functions centered on their center frequencies and added together (160 and 320 iirc), they can modulate frequency alongside the amplitude (I'm imagine they're basically truncating a fourier series at the first step and adjusting the biggest contributor (around 160 and 320) at each sampled window) whereas ADPCM has still a fixed sampling frequency of a real signal (and logaritmically adjusts the amplitude in steps like nintendo does). If anything it's possible that there are more center frequencies in hd rumble 2.
Didn't we found other wave forms?
I know that rumble sent to joycons is not the same as the data from the game
is interpolated at some point
Idk, not sure about that

What I'm pretty confident is that hd rumble is supposed to define two discrete waves (be them squared, triangular, sinusoidal or whatever) changing their amplitude and frequency at fixed intervals, not providing a high and low band of a real signal sampled at a fixed frequency
otherwise frequency modulation would be unnecessary and the bandwidth needed would be much more, even considering adpcm

on signals that have only two major components, they could kinda match I guess, but it's nowhere near the flexibility or the quality of a real pcm implementation, but then again our output device is a motor, not a speaker
the samples you found are likely part of a wave that can be stretched in frequency and amplitude when needed for those I'd believe

All that aside, the data is packed into outgoing reports at runtime. The vibration data is sampled at a different rate to which the controller is sending reports, so it can send more than one vibration sample at a time, and is (lossily) encoded accordingly to fit within the available space
Regardless of what it represents, the data found in games is not going to be 1:1 with what you see in the outgoing reports
I think there's a pre-encoded file format for storing vibrations, but it's probably also not infeasible to generate it dynamically

messages.content: I think in any case it's safe to say that anything outside the SoC is going to be encrypted
Probably need to perform hardware exploits to get access unless Nintendo have been nice enough to leave us a memory read command
Our best bet might be waiting to see if anyone can exploit the console to the point of dumping sysmodules from RAM. Then we could take a look in the code for the presence of unseen commands

In fact, I don’t understand why dekuNukem can find commands like FEATURE 0x72: Memory read. After all, such commands are not usually used when the Console and Joy-Con communicate, so it is impossible to capture the packets.
If you reverse the hid module you can see the code that uses them
According to the following information, they should have directly decompiled the unencrypted firmware and discovered this command.
I haven't looked at the timeline, but I imagine a lot of his findings came after we were able to dump and decrypt the console firmware
Yes, it's highly likely this was the case. I have reversed some of the code myself because I was interested in how firmware updates worked
It's also possible he just sniffed the communication. I think you can do OTA updates over USB too
Have you reverse engineered some of the Joy-Con2 code?
No, nothing has been dumped publicly
All our work is based off of sniffing either USB or BLE between the console and the controller
I think the original OTA updates write the firmware and then read it back to verify it was correctly written
He may also have been looking at UART I guess
They've definitely put more effort into securing it this time around
Maybe. The update package captured by BLE uses a different handle command and is longer. It may contain a memory read command.
I don't think I saw anything that looked like a read, but I only skimmed through the capture
Might be possible to try fuzzing the command handle for new commands. I haven't paid much attention to what happens if you send a malformed command
There's not necessarily any need for a read command this time around though. I'm pretty sure all the protocols in use guarantee data integrity
Yes, the memory read command has not been captured yet. I think it may exist like you.
Firmware cracking is the most difficult, but it is necessary to get a glimpse of the full picture of Joy-Con.
Yes, having the controller firmware is the best outcome. But I think we could get a decent picture from having a dump of the hid module from the console too
I've learnt more about Switch 1 controllers from that than the controller firmware
Not to say it's not a better source of info, I just wasn't able to get it decompiled properly 😅
In some ways it's easier on the console side too, because all the known IPC calls give a lot of nice hints when reversing what the code does

Yes, I also learned a lot from dekuNukem's project. It is currently impossible to crack the firmware, but I feel that if you don't crack the firmware, you won't be able to understand the BLE pairing handshake process.
I heard that the dock of Switch 2 has been cracked. I wonder if the handshake protocol algorithm of the dock is the same as that of the controller.
Maybe, but unless the firmwares contain some kind of pre-shared key material I think we probably have enough info to reconstruct the process from having code for _either_ side of the exchange
Obviously having the controller firmware is easier, because we could just copy the code that generates the reply and be done
But the console side has to a) generate a challenge, and b) verify a response. It also seems to be the side responsible for deciding the LTK. In some ways it may actually be more valuable
At the very least it would provide some additional clues
I think it's more plausible we get access to that first unless there's someone out there interested in eg. glitching the controller
I lack the tools and experience to give it a try unfortunately

Not personally, but we've documented the format
There's no "request", it just sends them as part of the input format

```
| Offset | Size | Value                | Comment                                                      |
| ---    | ---  | ---                  | ---                                                          |
| 0x0    | 0x1  | Counter              |                                                              |
| 0x1    | 0x1  | Unknown              | Power info?                                                  |
| 0x2    | 0x3  | Buttons              |                                                              |
| 0x5    | 0x3  | Left Analog Stick    |                                                              |
| 0x8    | 0x3  | Right Analog Stick   |                                                              |
| 0xB    | 0x1  | Unknown              | Always 0x38                                                  |
| 0xC    | 0x1  | Left Analog Trigger  | Only present on Gamecube NSO controller                      |
| 0xD    | 0x1  | Right Analog Trigger | Only present on Gamecube NSO controller                      |
| 0xD    | 0x1  | Headset/Flags        | Only present on Pro Controller. 0x1 when headset inserted    |
| 0xE    | 0x1  | Motion Data Length   | Length of following motion data. Observed values {0, 30, 40} |
| 0xF    | 0x28 | Motion Data          | Activated via feature bit 2                                  |
| 0x37   | 0x8  | -                    | Reserved                                                     |
```
That's the common format used by USB and BLE (handle 0x000E)
There's also another BLE format on handle 0x000A
This is probably available on USB too, but you'd have to request it somehow. So far nobody has seen it in use AFAIK

Yo! I just stumbled across the repo, just wanted to say nice work! I've wanted to help write a driver for the joycon2s. Is there any way one could emulate the pairing handshake with a generic bluetooth card?
In what context? Connecting the controller to a PC? Emulating the controller for use with a switch 2?

In short, yeah it's possible but a) depends on the OS and what the Bluetooth stack/API allows for and b) ~~we don't understand how one of the key exchange command's data is generated so can't replicate it currently~~ see the messages below 😉
Ok, so I've cracked the 0x15 command pairing exchange
1) The console sends command 0x15, 0x01 with a list of host bluetooth addresses
2) The console generates a random 16-byte key (A1) and sends it via command 0x15, 0x04
3) The controller responds with its own 16-byte key  (B1, seems to always be 5CF6EE792CDF05E1BA2B6325C41A5F10)
4) A1 ^ B1 produces the LTK
5) The console generates a second 16 byte key (A2) and sends it via command 0x15, 0x02
6) The controller computes the response (B2) by encrypting  A2  with the LTK using AES-ECB and sends it to the console
The key to that last step is that both the LTK and A2 are _byte reversed_
Oh, and 7) the pairing is finalised and committed to flash by sending command 0x15, 0x03

Pairing is the act of exchanging the key material
As in, it always will try to pair to the controller in the background, even without the users request to connect
That's essentially how all LE reconnection works. It's scanning in the background, just generally with a lower frequency than an active scan
But it typically only works for paired devices

But the controller sends different advertisements for reconnect and pairing, so the console can differentiate
As can any custom driver running on the PC side
And reconnect is only considered for paired or at least authorised devices

`OP_READ_BY_GRP_TYPE_REQ` is sent when enumerating both the primary and secondary services, the difference is the handle you use (the 0x2800 vs 0x2801 you mentioned)

First the primary services are discovered, then when there are no more the secondary ones are discovered. Once both sets are done(even if secondary request fails with an error) included service discovery starts.

So instead of treating it as an error during secondary discovery, the whole process times out and the device is disconnected again

Command 0x01 is not NFC. Is the MCU. As I said before MCU is the middle man between the switch and nfc. They changed all the numbers from sw1 but I figured out the most important ones 

Subcommand 0x05 reads the MCU status. Basically to know what the mcu is doing in any given time. It also let's you know the tag status
Subcommand 0x06 read device. Sends a read command to the device you configured. In this case NFC. This is where you request the read blocks of the tag
Subcommand 0x08 writedevice. Sends a write command to the device you configured. In this case NFC. This is used to write data into the tag
Subcommand 0x14 write buffer. You fill the buffer here to write stuff to the tag
Subcommand 0x15 read buffer. This is the actual reply of the NFC device. You read the tag data here.

- Values change with orientation, not speed, so its not velocity

The gyro data seems to baked into some quaternion that only tracks pitch and tilt.

It is a self clocking signal that oscillates back and forth between two states. In the A state, G0 (blue line) sweeps a full u26 range, in the B state G2 (organe line) sweeps maxval(u24) downto 0. When G0 hits maxval in A or G2 hits minval in B, the signal resets and switches state.

The base signals are some mx+t (hence the impression of a timestamp), but there is some bending, I suspect some arcsin component, that makes the signal slower in the middle and faster at the boundaries. I expect that is engineered so that the system spends less time near boundaries.

The A phase takes ~300 seconds, the B phase a little longer.  I have been following the idea that the quaternion value scales the signals, but I cannot put it together.

It would seem when we turn on a controller, it initializes this quaternion once, probably to (1,0,0,0), and then keeps rotating the thing. This means every recording one makes is relative to the position of the controller when it was switched on. This makes me believe there is a command we can send to the controller to reset its quaternion, because everything else would lead to many weired situations during gaming.

The quaternion is somehow modulated onto these base signals. I have been suspecting it a) scales the base signals on phase change and b) changes to the quaternion, i.e. movement, change the signals slopes.

hi all!! I'm curious about the interval speed at which the joycons send data to the switch over bluetooth. from what i can see the og joycons use standard bluetooth at a rate of 15ms per packet, but the switch 2s cant be found on anything other than a BLE connection, and are set to 60ms per packet. I was wondering if anyone had some info on getting them to send at a faster interval rate, or connecting them over br/edr instead

With BLE the server and client negotiate the connection interval to use for updates. This determines the maximum rate at which a device can send inputs. The Switch 2 console uses an interval of 15ms by default, but switches to 5ms once the device is paired. This value is smaller than the minimum 7.5ms defined in the Bluetooth spec
Since you mention 60ms, I assume you're on Windows. I did some digging in the windows Bluetooth driver and found this to be the default interval used

Usually the peripheral would send a preferred connection parameters request containing a connection interval value, and the host would adjust the connection interval as it sees fit. Switch 2 controllers never send this request as the console uses a special vendor command to explicitly set the values instead, so the value never gets updated from the default. This is why you'll get 60ms on Windows

On Windows 10 (and below, I guess) there doesn't seem to be any public API allowing the value to be set manually. The only way it updates is in response to the parameter update request. I messed around with the registry and found it's possible to manually inject a pairing entry for the controller where you insert "cached" connection interval values, which windows will use instead of the defaults when establishing the connection. This will allow you to get you close to the real rate, but you won't be able to use a value below the official 7.5ms
On Windows 11 there is a WinRT API call that can set the connection parameters, but it needs to be called manually
Similar likely applies to other OSes, but the default connection interval used may differ
